初學先認識兩種常見型：傳統繩調音型配黑色鼓皮，多用於多明尼加民俗音樂；現代螺栓調: Begin by getting to know the two common types: the traditional rope-tuned type with black heads, mostly used in Dominican folk music; and the modern bolt-tuned type with conga heads, whose metal or wooden rim can be struck as rhythmic filler and which, struck correctly, sounds something like a wood block, and which can also be tuned up towards a conga. Start with three basic strokes: slap, rim/woodblock and open tone, and fit them into standard merengue rhythms such as merengue derecho and pambiche. In a typical merengue / perico ripiao the tambora has to play many rhythms and variations of them; in orchestra merengue it usually plays only merengue derecho, as background.

坦博拉鼓名稱源自西班牙語tambor，意為鼓，為雙面膜鳴鼓，主要用於梅倫格音樂。: The name of the tambora comes from the Spanish tambor, meaning drum. It is a two-headed membranophone, used mainly in merengue. Its development is closely bound up with Dominican folk music: the older form is rope-tuned with black heads and is common in folk music, while modern makers use bolt tuning and conga heads and can tune it higher. In the past, in the Dominican Republic and elsewhere, the shell was often made from salvaged rum barrels. A player is called a tamborero. In the development of merengue it took an important rhythmic role in typical merengue (also called perico ripiao), and later became mostly background in orchestral merengue.
坦博拉鼓用於梅倫格音樂，在多明尼加民俗音樂中可見較古老的繩調式鼓。於梅倫格提皮科: The tambora is used in merengue, and in Dominican folk music you can still see the older rope-tuned drum. In merengue típico (also called perico ripiao, the oldest form of merengue) it carries a large share of the rhythms and their variations; in orchestral merengue it is mostly background, with the main rhythm taken by the congas and then the güira. Orchestral merengue often has a separate timbales player, while in perico ripiao the same player usually plays both timbales and tambora.
坦博拉鼓音色深沉而富有穿透力，具有溫暖且厚重的質感。其低頻特徵明顯，音域集中在中: The tambora's timbre is deep and carries well, with a warm, heavy body. Its low frequencies stand out and the range sits in the low middle, so it can give out a full, powerful drum sound. The heads' vibration produces a deep resonance rich in harmonics, and the sound sustains and rings well. Next to a Western drum kit the tambora is fuller and calmer; next to African drums its sound is warmer. By varying where and how they strike, players can produce many shades, from a low muffled tone to a brighter clear one. These resonant qualities let it carry the rhythmic foundation in Caribbean music and blend well with the other percussion.
坦博拉鼓鼓身採用實心木材製造，通常選用杉木或其他硬木，提供堅實的共鳴腔體。鼓膜由: The shell of the tambora is made of solid wood, usually cedar or another hardwood, which gives a firm resonance chamber. The heads are of natural animal skin, mostly calfskin or goatskin, specially treated to make it tougher and better sounding. The edge of the head is bound to a wooden hoop with cord or leather straps, to adjust tension and pitch. Metal fittings strengthen the hoop and its stability, and some high-end instruments use brass or iron reinforcing rings.
坦博拉鼓（Tambora Dominicana）是兩面鼓，屬膜鳴樂器，名稱源自西: The tambora (Tambora Dominicana) is a two-headed drum, a membranophone, its name coming from the Spanish word for drum. It is common in the merengue of the Dominican Republic and elsewhere, and players are called tamboreros. The traditional type is rope-tuned with black heads and is more often found in Dominican folk music; the modern type is bolt-tuned with conga heads, its metal or wooden rim struck as rhythmic filler, and its pitch can be raised to approach a conga. It is common in merengue típico and orchestra merengue, and is played with strokes such as the slap and the rim.
